items.stem: A nurse prepares to enter the room of a client with suspected Clostridioides difficile infection.
items.scenarioText: The client has profuse watery diarrhea and is placed on contact precautions.
items.leadInQuestion: Which personal protective equipment should the nurse use before entering the room?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mask and sterile gloves only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gown and gloves

choices.label: C
choices.text: N95 respirator and eye shield

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical cap and shoe covers

items.explanation: Contact precautions for C. difficile require gown and gloves on room entry to reduce organism transmission.
items.rationale: C. difficile spreads by spores on contaminated surfaces and hands, so barrier protection against contact exposure is required.

distractorRationale.A: A mask is not routinely required for contact precautions, and sterile gloves are unnecessary for basic room entry.
distractorRationale.C: An N95 respirator is used for airborne precautions, not routine contact isolation for C. difficile.
distractorRationale.D: Caps and shoe covers do not address the main transmission route for this organism.

learningObjectives: Apply contact precaution principles for enteric infections
items.sourceReferenceTitle: Isolation precautions and enteric pathogen review

items.stem: A nurse is teaching unlicensed assistive personnel how to prevent patient falls during hourly rounds.
items.scenarioText: The unit has had several unwitnessed falls during night shift.
items.leadInQuestion: Which actions should the nurse include in the instruction? Select all that apply.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place frequently used items within the client's reach

choices.label: B
choices.text: Keep the bed in the lowest position when the client is resting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raise all four side rails for every high-risk client

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ensure the call light is visible and functioning

choices.label: E
choices.text: Encourage the client to get up without assistance to build strength

items.explanation: Fall prevention includes environmental safety and prompt access to assistance, not restraint-like measures or unsupervised ambulation.
items.rationale: Keeping essentials close, lowering the bed, and maintaining call light access reduce unsafe self-transfer attempts.

distractorRationale.C: Raising all four side rails can function as a restraint and may increase injury risk.
distractorRationale.E: High-risk clients should request help before ambulating rather than getting up alone.

items.sourceReferenceTitle: Patient safety and falls prevention review

items.stem: A postoperative client has an indwelling urinary catheter. The drainage bag is hanging below the bladder and the tubing shows no kinks.
items.scenarioText: The nurse notes cloudy urine and wants to reduce catheter-associated infection risk.
items.leadInQuestion: Which action should the nurse take first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obtain a routine urine specimen from the drainage bag

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer clinically necessary

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disconnect the tubing daily to cleanse the catheter junction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Irrigate the catheter every shift with sterile saline

items.explanation: The most effective prevention step for CAUTI is prompt removal of an unnecessary indwelling catheter.
items.rationale: Limiting catheter duration reduces bacterial entry and biofilm formation more effectively than routine irrigation or disconnection.

distractorRationale.A: Specimens should not be taken from the drainage bag because this increases contamination risk and does not prevent infection.
distractorRationale.C: Breaking the closed system increases infection risk.
distractorRationale.D: Routine irrigation is not recommended unless specifically prescribed for a clinical indication.

learningObjectives: Prioritize interventions that reduce CAUTI risk

items.stem: A nurse is preparing medications for two clients in semi-private rooms when another client activates the call bell reporting shortness of breath.
items.scenarioText: The nurse has not yet administered the medications and is alone in the medication room.
items.leadInQuestion: Which action is the nurse's priority?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Finish preparing both clients' medications to avoid interruption errors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Assess the client reporting shortness of breath immediately

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ask the charge nurse to document the event before assessing the client

choices.label: D
choices.text: Administer the medications, then check the client when done

items.explanation: Actual airway and breathing concerns take priority over medication preparation tasks.
items.rationale: Shortness of breath may indicate immediate deterioration, so the nurse should stop and assess the client first.

distractorRationale.A: Continuing medication preparation delays care for a potentially unstable client.
distractorRationale.C: Documentation is not the initial priority during a possible respiratory emergency.
distractorRationale.D: Medication administration can wait while urgent physiologic needs are evaluated.

learningObjectives: Prioritize care using airway, breathing, circulation principles

items.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer insulin to a client with diabetes before breakfast.
items.scenarioText: Another nurse is available to assist with verification.
items.leadInQuestion: Which action best supports medication safety before administration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ask another nurse to independently verify the insulin type and dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Document the medication as given before injection to save time

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leave the syringe at the bedside while checking the breakfast tray

choices.label: D
choices.text: Skip client identification if the nurse cared for the client yesterday

items.explanation: High-alert medications such as insulin require careful verification to reduce dosage and product errors.
items.rationale: Independent double-checks help catch high-risk medication errors before they reach the client.

distractorRationale.B: Medication documentation should occur after administration, not before.
distractorRationale.C: Prepared medications should remain under direct nurse control to prevent mix-ups.
distractorRationale.D: Every administration requires standard client identification checks.

learningObjectives: Apply medication administration safety checks for high-alert drugs
items.sourceReferenceTitle: Medication safety essentials for nursing review

items.stem: A nurse is reinforcing discharge teaching for a client recovering from influenza at home.
items.scenarioText: The client asks how to reduce spreading infection to family members.
items.leadInQuestion: Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wash hands frequently with soap and water or sanitizer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Share drinking glasses only after rinsing them with water

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clean commonly touched surfaces regularly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop prescribed antiviral medication once fever improves

items.explanation: Respiratory hygiene, hand hygiene, and surface cleaning reduce household spread of influenza.
items.rationale: Transmission decreases when secretions are contained, contaminated hands are cleaned, and shared surfaces are disinfected.

distractorRationale.C: Shared personal items can transmit infection even if only rinsed with water.
distractorRationale.E: Prescribed medication should be completed as directed unless the provider changes the plan.

learningObjectives: Teach infection prevention measures for home care
